title: Esp32Tap safety: the 4s manual-lease deadman emergency-stops an idle belt, and the fault it latches is unrecoverable
description:
TWO OPEN CONTROL-TIER DEFECTS, restated because they were the mechanism behind an intermittent that cost a full investigation in the coach gate.

(1) A manual command (POST /api/speed, a BLE Control Point write, the coach) takes LeaseExpiry::Manual(now + 4s). NOTHING renews it: the C++ design assumed an owner heartbeat over the websocket, and this firmware's HTTP surface sends none. So a user who sets a speed and starts walking is emergency-stopped 4s later with no client fault. test_reviewer_attacks.py::test_a_manual_speed_command_survives_ten_seconds is that, red by design.

(2) That emergency_stop('lease_expired') is immediately followed by proxy_feedback_invalid (the contacts have not released by the time the mode is already PROXY), which sets fault_latched — and fault_latched is set in eight places and cleared in NONE. request_emulate then refuses forever. ONE ordinary user action permanently removes the device's ability to drive the belt until it is power-cycled, and every later command still answers 200. test_reviewer_attacks.py::test_e_a_latched_fault_is_recoverable.

WHY IT IS FILED AGAIN NOW: it is not only a bench-safety issue, it makes gates nondeterministic. test_coach.py::test_a_truncated_reply_produces_no_action asserted a manually commanded speed several seconds after setting it, across an unbounded number of emulated-ESP32 TLS handshakes, and failed roughly 1 run in 3 under load for this reason and not for any reason to do with the coach. 55f592b re-aimed that assertion at the wire and required a lease_expired audit receipt before tolerating a zeroed belt, but the defect itself is untouched.

DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED IN 55f592b: SafetyController is compared op-for-op against the C++ core and safety_model.py by the difftest gate, so changing lease semantics is a change to the compared contract and needs its own deliberate act with the owner awake. The candidate fixes are (a) an owner heartbeat from the firmware while a /ws client is connected, (b) LeaseExpiry::NoDeadline for the HTTP surface with the emulate 3-hour timeout as the real deadman, or (c) an /api/reset route that clears a latched fault — all three are contract changes, not patches.

title: Esp32Tap coach: stop_treadmill reports 'treadmill stopped' for a belt it did not stop
description:
net/coach.rs:552-557 routes Action::StopTreadmill to ProgramState::stop() and nothing else. With no program running that is an EMPTY plan, drive(plan,true) releases only the EXECUTOR lease, and a manually commanded belt (HTTP surface) keeps its lease and its speed.

That half is the known open defect the HTTP endpoint shares (test_reviewer_attacks.py::test_b_program_stop_zeroes_a_manually_commanded_belt, red by design). What is NEW and belongs to the coach tier is the SENTENCE: describe() runs BEFORE apply() (coach.rs:469-476) and apply returns an override only on failure — StopTreadmill has no failure branch — so the transcript says 'treadmill stopped'.

net/coach.rs:466-468 claims 'THE SAME CLAMPED VALUE IS DESCRIBED AND APPLIED. One rendering, so what the user is told and what the belt was asked for cannot diverge.' Here they diverge, in the direction that matters: the user asked the coach to stop the treadmill, was told it stopped, and the relay is still closed with the belt commanded at 3.0 mph.

MEASURED against the current image:
  COACH SAID [{'name':'stop_treadmill','args':{},'result':'treadmill stopped'}]
  DEVICE STATUS {... 'speed': 3.0, 'relay': True, 'mode': 'emulate' ...}

Fix: stop_treadmill must reach the belt itself (control::command(Surface::Http, 0, incline) after the program stop, or a shared 'stop everything' helper), and the description must come from the OUTCOME rather than from the action.

repro: env -C hardware/Esp32Tap/firmware/esp32_rs/tools/qemu_scenarios python3 -m pytest test_coach_review.py -q -k manually_commanded_belt -s

title: Esp32Tap BOM: align module to N8R8 (PSRAM) — dev kit has PSRAM, production BOM does not
description:
MISMATCH: dev hardware is ESP32-S3-DEVKITC-1-N8R8 (Digi-Key 1965-ESP32-S3-DEVKITC-1-N8R8-ND) = 8MB flash + 8MB octal PSRAM, but tools/design.py specifies ESP32-S3-WROOM-1-N8 (8MB flash, NO PSRAM) in two places (design.py:91 and :1392). Developing against 8MB PSRAM and shipping a no-PSRAM module means firmware that fits on the bench fails at hardware bring-up.

FIX: change the module to ESP32-S3-WROOM-1-N8R8 and regenerate. This is a DROP-IN: identical WROOM-1 footprint/pinout, and octal PSRAM's GPIO35/36/37 are already ('U1','28'/'29'/'30') = no_connect in our design, so there is no pin conflict and NO layout/gerber change. Requires: BOM/CPL regeneration, JLC stock + DFM re-check (tools/check_jlc_stock.py), full make check.

FIRMWARE CONSEQUENCES: enable CONFIG_SPIRAM (octal, check errata for speed/config); be EXPLICIT about placement — with CONFIG_SPIRAM_USE_MALLOC ordinary malloc can silently return PSRAM, and PSRAM is SPI-attached + cached so the serial hot path and safety core must pin to MALLOC_CAP_INTERNAL (SRAM); route mbedTLS + WiFi/lwIP buffers to PSRAM (CONFIG_MBEDTLS_EXTERNAL_MEM_ALLOC, CONFIG_SPIRAM_TRY_ALLOCATE_WIFI_LWIP). PSRAM makes the budget generous, NOT infinite — the allocate-at-boot-only / reject-don't-OOM discipline still stands.

TESTING: esp-QEMU 9.2.2 has an ssi_psram device and a machine memory option, so the committed QEMU harness can run the shipped PSRAM config — do not let dev and prod configs diverge.

title: Esp32Tap QEMU sweep intermittents — likely concurrent-session interference, not the firmware
description:
SYMPTOM (as first reported): `program` gate intermittent under -n4. Passed two
plain sweeps, failed the DEEP sweep at the same commit with zero tree changes:
test_program.py::test_repeated_manual_commands_do_not_cycle_the_relay raised
"UART1 TX never contained b'[hmph:C8]'" with a 0-byte UART1 capture.

THAT SYMPTOM WAS MISLEADING AND IS NOW FIXED (commit 9e65d09). The test waited
for `relay_cmd_on` and then for wire bytes. `relay_cmd_on` proves emulate entry
BEGAN, not that it finished, so a fail-closed entry looked identical to a dead
capture thread thirty seconds later. `assert_emulate_entry_completed` now
asserts `feedback_emulate_stable` at the entry and reports the transfer events
since the command, treating an abort as terminal.

REPRODUCED with that diagnostic in place, once, under heavy host CPU contention
(a container build running concurrently with -n4):

    audit event not seen: 'feedback_emulate_stable' (since 3)

i.e. `relay_cmd_on` fired and the 10 ms relay-feedback window never qualified.

MECHANISM (established by reading, all four facts verified in source):

  1. safety/constants.rs: RELAY_FEEDBACK_DEADLINE_US = 10_000 (10 ms), with
     RELAY_FEEDBACK_STABLE_US = 1_000 and FEEDBACK_POLL_US = 200. The shim's
     K1 model adds a break-before-make transit, so a healthy qualification
     lands around +3 ms and the slack is ~7 ms.
  2. The deadline is measured with `Esp32Clock::now()` ->
     `esp_timer_get_time()` -> the systimer, which esp-QEMU drives from
     QEMU_CLOCK_VIRTUAL. The harness runs QEMU WITHOUT `-icount`, and with
     icount off QEMU_CLOCK_VIRTUAL is HOST WALL TIME.
  3. Progress through the window is measured by `RomDelay::delay_us(200)` ->
     `esp_rom_delay_us`, a ROM busy-wait that advances with the CPU cycle
     counter — GUEST INSTRUCTION TIME.
  4. So the budget is spent in wall time and consumed in instruction time.
     When the host deschedules the QEMU process mid-window, wall time keeps
     running and instruction time does not: the deadline expires before the
     poll loop has taken its samples, `enforce_due_safety` latches a fault with
     `entry_feedback_timeout`, the relay drops and the belt transmits nothing.
     On real silicon both clocks are the same silicon and the divergence cannot
     occur.

THE FIRMWARE IS NOT AT FAULT. 10 ms is the hardware-derived relay-feedback
deadline from the Python safety model (relay_feedback_seconds = 0.01) and
must not be loosened; failing closed is the correct behaviour for a transfer
whose feedback did not qualify. The busy-wait is deliberate — the comment on
`RomDelay` records that a `vTaskDelay` would round to a 1 ms tick and make the
deadline unsatisfiable.

FREQUENCY: 1 occurrence in ~45 runs of test_program.py -n4 observed here, and
the only one occurred while a docker build was saturating the host. 0 in ~30
runs on an idle machine (-n4 and -n8). The reviewer's original hit was in a
full sweep.

CANDIDATE FIX, DELIBERATELY NOT APPLIED: run QEMU with `-icount shift=auto`,
which makes QEMU_CLOCK_VIRTUAL instruction-counted and decouples guest time
from host load entirely — eliminating the class rather than reducing its
probability. NOT applied because (a) it is a change to
tools/qemu_harness/qemu_session.py, which is byte-locked to the C++ tier's copy
by tools/verify_harness_copy.py and would need a new pinned entry in
ALLOWED_STRENGTHENING; (b) icount serialises TCG and its cost on ~22 scenarios
is unmeasured; (c) every scenario's timing is currently tuned against a
wall-clock guest, so it is a GLOBAL change to the meaning of every gate, made
on a defect that fires roughly once in 45 runs. It wants a measured decision,
not a 3 a.m. one.

DO NOT "FIX" THIS BY: raising the 10 ms deadline, adding a retry around the
entry, sleeping before the assertion, or lowering -n. All four hide a real
divergence between two clocks and none removes it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
SECOND MEMBER OF THE SAME FAMILY, found 2026-07-29 in a DEEP sweep:
`profiles` FAILED where it had passed both plain sweeps at the same commit.

    test_app_can_get_past_the_profile_picker
    urllib.error.URLError: <urlopen error [SSL: UNEXPECTED_EOF_WHILE_READING]>

and on the guest console, at the same instant:

    E (3360) esp_https_server: esp_tls_create_server_session failed, 0xffff7ff7
    E (3361) httpd: httpd_accept_conn: session creation failed

0xffff7ff7 is -0x8009 = -ESP_ERR_ESP_TLS_SERVER_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT (32777,
confirmed against the generated bindings). The device DELIBERATELY dropped a
handshake: `net/http.rs` sets `tls_handshake_timeout_ms = 500`, which — because
the socket is blocking with `recv_wait_timeout = 1` — grants a peer exactly ONE
second of silence mid-handshake before the single httpd worker is taken back.
That budget is a measured safety parameter: at the IDF default (10 s) one idle
socket pushed `POST /api/program/stop` from 0.25 s to 15.25 s with the belt
moving.

So the shape is identical to the relay-feedback case: a hard, deliberate,
safety-motivated GUEST-SIDE wall-clock budget against a counterpart whose
progress depends on HOST scheduling — there, guest instruction time; here, the
Python client's own scheduling. The device is behaving as specified in both.

NOT REPRODUCED on demand: 10/10 passes in isolation, 5/5 under 40 spinning CPU
hogs. 1 failure in 1 DEEP sweep; 0 in 2 plain sweeps.

MITIGATION APPLIED (attribution only, no tolerance): `tools/qemu_scenarios/
httpc.py` now reads the guest console when a handshake fails and, if the device
logged that exact refusal, re-raises naming it, the budget, the likely cause
and the instruction not to raise the budget. Nothing is retried and no
assertion is weakened; an HTTPError (a real 4xx/5xx answer) still passes
through untouched. Before this, the failure surfaced as
`UNEXPECTED_EOF_WHILE_READING`, which reads like a crashed server.

DO NOT "FIX" THIS BY: raising tls_handshake_timeout_ms, retrying the request,
or enabling lru_purge. The first is the measured belt-availability regression
above; the second hides a real refusal; the third makes a burst evict a live
client instead of being refused, which net/http.rs rejects by design.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
THIRD SIGHTING, same DEEP sweep session, 2026-07-29: `adversar` FAILED at
test_quick_start_from_idle_works with

    idle quick-start never moved the belt; {... 'mode': 'proxy',
    'relay': False, 'fault': True, ...}

`fault: True` is a LATCHED FAULT, which is the `entry_feedback_timeout`
signature from member 1 above (that path sets `fault_latched = true` before
emergency-stopping). Mode back to Proxy, relay released, zero bytes on the
motor wire — the belt can never move again in that state, because
`enforce_due_safety` refuses every subsequent motion.

NOT CONFIRMED, AND THE REASON IS ITSELF A FINDING: the cause could not be read
off the dump. The device's audit ring is EVENT_CAPACITY = 256 entries and
`complete_console_frame` is pushed at the pacer's rate, so by the time the
45 s `_belt_reaches` timeout expired the fault-latching event had been EVICTED
by console-frame traffic. `debug_dump` shows only the last 40 audit events and
all 40 were console frames. This is the same eviction hazard
`tasks/serial_engine.rs` already documents for VBUS_PRESENT_N ("calling it
every 5 ms would push 200 events/s and wrap the 256-slot audit ring in ~1.3 s,
EVICTING emergency and fault events") — it applies to complete_console_frame
too whenever a scenario runs a pacer for tens of seconds.

MITIGATION APPLIED (attribution only): `_belt_reaches` in test_adversarial.py
now checks `/api/status` for `fault` on every poll and raises IMMEDIATELY when
it is set, printing the non-console audit events and naming this bead. A
latched fault is terminal, so waiting out the remaining timeout could never
have succeeded — it only destroyed the evidence. This fails EARLIER and more
loudly; no bound was shortened in the success direction and nothing is retried.

RUNNING TALLY: 3 failures, all in DEEP or full sweeps, all in different gates
(program / profiles / adversar), NONE reproducible in isolation (0 in ~30 runs
of program, 10/10 profiles, 5/5 profiles under 40 CPU hogs, 3/3 adversar's
quick-start cases). Two plain sweeps were 24/24 green back to back, twice.

`tools/sweep.sh` and `tools/check_unsafe_budget.py`, and building. Timestamps:

  sweep B  finished 07:41:05  — coach_core appeared at 07:40:35   ALL GREEN
  DEEP     started  ~07:41:30 — fully overlapped                  memreview FAIL

Three independent ways that breaks a run, none of them a firmware defect:

  1. CPU. A container build (docker + cargo + LLVM) alongside four QEMU guests
     is exactly the starvation the mechanism above needs. This is the ambient
     load I could not reproduce by hand with spinning loops — a real build is
     far more disruptive than a busy-wait, because it competes for memory
     bandwidth and I/O as well as cycles.
  2. SHARED BUILD ARTEFACT. Every QemuSession merges
     `build_qemu_test/esp32tap.bin` into its flash image at container start.
     Another session running `tools/build.sh` rewrites that file underneath.
     CLAUDE.md already records this exact lesson: "'CPU starvation' on a
     20-core machine turned out to be a TOCTOU in port allocation and a shared
     flash image two sessions raced on."
  3. THE SWEEP SCRIPT ITSELF WAS EDITED WHILE RUNNING. bash reads a script
     incrementally by byte offset, so editing `sweep.sh` mid-run can make it
     execute the wrong bytes. The other session added a `coachcore` gate to it
     while my DEEP sweep was executing.

SO: the MECHANISM described above is still correct about WHAT the device did —
`-0x8009` is definitively ESP_ERR_ESP_TLS_SERVER_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT, and a
latched fault is definitively terminal. But the TRIGGER is now most likely
CONCURRENT-SESSION INTERFERENCE, not ambient host scheduling. That changes the
remedy completely:

  * DO NOT reach for `-icount` first. It is a global change to the meaning of
    every gate, aimed at a cause that may not be the operative one.
  * FIRST: re-run DEEP on a QUIET tree — no other session building, no other
    session editing esp32_rs — and see whether it reproduces at all. That is
    one 17-minute experiment and it discriminates cleanly.
  * If it does NOT reproduce quietly, the real defect is that the harness has
    no interlock against a second session rebuilding the image it is booting.
    A per-run snapshot of build_qemu_test/ (or a flock on it, like the port
    leases already use) would close it, and that is a much smaller, safer
    change than icount.

EVIDENCE THAT SUPPORTS THE CONTAMINATION READING: every failure was in a long
full/DEEP sweep (8-17 min, maximum overlap window) and NONE reproduced in
isolation — 0 in ~45 runs of test_program.py -n4, 10/10 test_profiles.py,
5/5 test_profiles.py under 40 spinning CPU hogs, 3/3 the adversarial
quick-start cases. Two consecutive CLEAN plain sweeps were 24/24 ALL GREEN.

title: Esp32Tap BLE: on-hardware verification outstanding — no radio has ever run
description:
ble_core (hardware/Esp32Tap/firmware/esp32_rs/ble_core/) ports the FTMS and HR
PROTOCOL logic from the working Pi daemons; esp32tap/src/ble/ is the NimBLE
radio tier on top of it. Sweep gates: `blecore` (host cases, ~1 s), `bledegrade`
(7 QEMU cases, ~36 s) and `blecp` (9 QEMU cases — the belt edge, added
2026-07-29).

WHAT IS PROVEN (host):
  * every characteristic's bytes (Treadmill Data 0x2ACD, Feature 0x2ACC,
    Speed Range 0x2AD4, Incline Range 0x2AD5, Training Status 0x2AD3,
    Machine Status 0x2ADA, Control Point 0x2AD9 response)
  * Control Point parsing total over untrusted input
  * km/h <-> mph conversion incl. the daemon's truncation; thousandths-of-a-mile
    -> metres for Total Distance; integer half-percent rounding == the daemon's
    float rule over all 65536 i16 values
  * ble_core::peer — a strap's advertised name cannot escape a JSON string, and
    a BLE address is rejected whole rather than half-parsed
  * the belt edge: a write becomes safety_core newtypes for control.rs (THE ONE
    PATH TO THE BELT), unclamped ABOVE the range and clamped to 0 BELOW it

WHAT IS PROVEN (QEMU, test_ble_degraded.py): with the radio REFUSED, the device
boots once, serves HTTPS, pushes /ws status+session+hr, moves the belt, and
answers all four /api/hrm* routes. The whole qemu-test image carries
--features ble, so all ~22 scenarios run against a radioless device.

WHAT IS PROVEN (QEMU, test_ble_control_point.py — added 2026-07-29): the ENTIRE
belt edge below the mbuf copy, driven through the qemu-test-only `QT ble_cp`
verb into the same `plan` -> `effect_of` -> `apply` -> `control::command` chain
`on_control_point` uses. A Stop lands while a program owns the lease and the
belt actually reaches zero; the lease comes back afterwards; a descent flattens
the belt; an out-of-range incline is refused and changes nothing; the km/h
conversion is wired; a zero-length write is INVALID_PARAM; malformed writes
never reach the belt or latch a fault; repeated writes do not cycle the relay.
The two Stop cases were RUN RED against the pre-fix image.

MEASURED MEMORY (same image, with vs without `ble`) — STATIC LINK COST ONLY:
  * app image      890 560 B -> 1 141 104 B   (+250 544 B; 54% of the 2 MB
                                               factory partition)
  * free internal RAM at heap_init
                   281 024 B -> 252 352 B     (-28 672 B = 28 KiB static)

NEW FINDING THAT CHANGED THE DESIGN: nimble_port_init does NOT return an error
when the controller cannot come up. Under esp-QEMU 9.2.2 (esp32s3) it
assert()s inside the closed-source BT blob -> panic -> SILENT_REBOOT -> the
relay drops mid-run, and the device reboot-looped every ~1.8 s. The mitigation
is a guard in FRONT of the call (ble::identity_address: the eFuse BT MAC must
be a factory unicast address — OUI != 00:00:00, multicast bit clear; QEMU
reports 00:00:00:00:00:02). The BLE task is also spawned last, lowest priority,
and deliberately NOT WDT-supervised (the watchdog's remedy is a reboot).

STILL NOT PROVEN, NEEDS A BOARD (QEMU HAS NO BLE RADIO):
  1. Every line of ble/ftms.rs and ble/central.rs past the identity guard is
     UNEXECUTED. No advertising, no connection, no pairing/bonding, no MTU
     negotiation, no notification, no indication has ever run. (The belt edge
     BELOW access_cb is now covered by test_ble_control_point.py; the mbuf copy
     itself and everything radio-side is not.)
  2. RUNTIME HEAP COST OF NIMBLE IS UNMEASURED and no number is quoted. The
     instrument exists: ble::bring_up logs `ble: heap cost N bytes (free X ->
     Y)` either side of nimble_port_init. FIRST THING TO CHECK ON HARDWARE —
     whether the stack fits alongside TLS + the app tier is an open question,
     and if it does not, say so with the number rather than ship a reboot.
  3. Whether the identity guard PASSES on a real ESP32-S3 (it must — every
     production part has the eFuse MAC programmed — but it has never been run
     on one, and a false negative there means no Bluetooth at all).
  4. FTMS Control Point -> control.rs ON REAL HARDWARE: that a peer's Set
     Target Speed actually moves the belt, and that an out-of-range write is
     refused with INVALID_PARAM rather than clamped. (The logic is now gated in
     QEMU; what is unproven is that a real ATT write reaches it.)
  5. HRM central end to end against a real chest strap: scan, the
     service/characteristic/CCCD discovery chain, and notifications reaching
     /api/hrm and the /ws hr frame.
  6. Peripheral + central SIMULTANEOUSLY on one radio (advertising FTMS while
     scanning/connected to a strap) with CONFIG_BT_NIMBLE_MAX_CONNECTIONS=2.
  7. No real client has connected: Zwift, QZ Fitness, Kinomap (the reason the
     idle alive-signal exists), Apple Watch, Garmin.
  8. The HRM strap address is RAM-only, not NVS — a known difference from the
     Pi's hrm_config.json; a strap must be re-picked after a power cycle.
     Decide on hardware whether that is acceptable.
  9. NIMBLE HOST TASK STACK HIGH-WATER MARK. The stack was UNSIZED until
     2026-07-29 (CONFIG_BT_NIMBLE_HOST_TASK_STACK_SIZE absent -> IDF default
     4096) on the task with the deepest untrusted call chain: access_cb ->
     on_control_point -> apply -> control::command -> apply_outputs, plus
     ~1100 B of logging buffers. It is now 8192 with the arithmetic written
     into sdkconfig.defaults (worst case ~4600 B), and ble::ftms samples
     uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark after every Control Point write, logging
     'ble: host task stack low-water N bytes' on each new minimum. READ THAT
     NUMBER ON THE FIRST BOARD and replace the arithmetic with it. An overflow
     here is a silent reboot and a reboot drops the relay mid-run — which is
     exactly how the httpd task failed in commit a055117.
 10. FREE HEAP CONVERGES ACROSS CONNECT/DISCONNECT CYCLES. Resident memory is
     required to be constant and independent of connection count, and nothing
     has ever connected. Needs >= 50 phone connect/disconnect cycles with the
     free heap sampled at each idle point, and heap_caps_get_free_size compared
     with 0, 1 and 2 links up.
 11. CCCD / SUBSCRIBE HANDLING IS UNEXECUTED. A BLE_GAP_EVENT_SUBSCRIBE arm was
     added 2026-07-29 (before it, the device notified peers that had subscribed
     to nothing, and never sent the daemon's on-subscribe initial Machine /
     Training Status). Confirm on hardware that a real client's CCCD write
     reaches it, that the initial values arrive, and that an unsubscribed peer
     now receives NO Treadmill Data.
 12. THE ADVERTISED NAME is back to the daemon's 'Precor 9.31' (it had been
     'esp32tap'). Confirm a phone with a remembered Pi device still finds it.

ACCEPTED RISK, RECORDED RATHER THAN LEFT IMPLICIT IN A MODULE COMMENT:
THE THREAT MODEL CHANGED IN THE PORT AND THE DOCS DID NOT SAY SO. On the Pi an
attacker needed LAN credentials to reach the FTMS daemon. Here the Control
Point (0x2AD9) is registered WRITE (not WRITE_ENC / WRITE_AUTHEN),
CONFIG_BT_NIMBLE_SM_LVL=0, no bonding, no NVS persistence, and advertising is
BLE_GAP_CONN_MODE_UND forever. So anything within ~10 m — no credential of any
kind — can write [0x02,lo,hi] and command up to 12.0 mph, [0x07] to resume the
retained speed, or [0x08,0x01] to stop a belt someone is running on. The
controller's clamps still hold (nothing exceeds 12.0 mph / 15%) and starting a
stationary belt at 12 mph is INSIDE the allowed envelope. Memory under this is
bounded (verified: retain_active evicts the previous same-connection identity
against a fixed array). This is inherited from the daemon and from the FTMS
spec, which mandates no pairing, and neither shipping client pairs. DECIDE ON
HARDWARE whether to require WRITE_ENC + bonding; it is a compatibility tradeoff
against Zwift/QZ/Kinomap, not a free win.

RELATED: the audit ring can be flushed by an unauthenticated peer. Each denied
Control Point write pushes two entries (connect + lease_rejected) into the
fixed EVENT_CAPACITY ring at ATT write rate, so the forensic record of why a
motion was refused can be overwritten from outside the building. Memory is
constant (the ring overwrites, never grows) and the belt is untouched. The
per-write LOG line is throttled (first, then 1 in 64) so the console cannot be
saturated; the ring itself is not, because not minting a generation for a write
that will be refused means a pre-check inside control::hold_lease — a second
opinion in front of THE ONE PATH TO THE BELT — which is not worth it for an
audit-churn fix without a test. Revisit with the lease work.

title: Esp32Tap TLS: esp_https_server missing from esp-idf-sys bindings
description:
net/tls.rs generates a self-signed EC P-256 identity and compiles, but nothing calls it: httpd_ssl_* produces ZERO symbols in the generated bindings, so httpd_ssl_start cannot be called.

TRIED AND REJECTED: [package.metadata.esp-idf-sys] esp_idf_components = [...] is an EXCLUSIVE whitelist. Naming esp_https_server + 4 others dropped every other component and the CMake build failed. Reverted.

NEXT ATTEMPT SHOULD START BY READING, NOT PROBING: esp-idf-sys supports a custom bindings header (it generates from a curated header list, not from every built component). Read its documented metadata keys once, then make ONE change. Each probe here costs a 60-180s rebuild, which is why serial experimentation was abandoned.

ALSO OPEN when this is picked up: the key is generated fresh every boot and NOT persisted to NVS, so the device identity changes on each restart. Tolerable while clients trust-all (TrustAllDelegate / trustAllTls) but it defeats trust-on-first-use, which the pending bearer-token decision (precor-9_3x-ds4) would rely on. TOFU cannot be honestly claimed until persistence lands.

DEFERRED BECAUSE: no board exists, clients trust-all, and every QEMU proof runs over HTTP, so TLS buys little today while costing open-ended build-system work. mDNS and the profile endpoints do not depend on it.

title: Voice: tap during SPEAKING leaves userActivated armed (zombie state)
description: VoiceViewModel.toggle() routes SPEAKING -> interrupt() which flushes audio and sets state=LISTENING, but does NOT clear userActivated. Every other deactivate path (LISTENING-tap, CONNECTING-tap, disconnect) clears it. Result: user taps mic mid-Gemini-response to deactivate, visually sees the icon transition past (purple SPEAKING -> green-pulse LISTENING), assumes voice is off; meanwhile mic is still armed (userActivated=true). Next status change (e.g., bumping incline) pushes context to Gemini via updateStateContext, Gemini emits an audio response, onAudioChunk's gate 'if (!userActivated) return' lets it through, audio plays unexpectedly. Two related zombie paths: line 362 (mic permission denied -> IDLE) and line 379 (teardownConnection -> IDLE) also leave userActivated=true. Fix (Option A from investigation): SPEAKING-tap is treated as deactivate everywhere else; mirror that. interrupt() becomes dead code (will be removed in a follow-up). Verify on tablet: tap mic, talk, while Gemini speaks tap again, confirm mic icon goes inactive (no green pulse), bump incline, no audio fires.
acceptance_criteria: In SPEAKING state, mic tap clears userActivated and goes to IDLE; mic icon shows inactive; bumping incline triggers no audible Gemini response. Same for line 362 + 379 paths.
close_reason: Two-part bug, both fixed: (1) tap during SPEAKING left userActivated armed (interrupt() path didn't deactivate); (2) server-side 'interrupted' signal arriving in response to silent context pushes (incline bumps) bounced voiceState back to LISTENING via the ungated onInterrupted callback, lighting the mic icon as 'active' even though audio was correctly dropped. Fix: SPEAKING toggle branch mirrors LISTENING (clear userActivated, flush, IDLE); onInterrupted now gated on userActivated; line 362 (mic perm fail) and line 379 (teardownConnection) also clear userActivated as belt-and-suspenders cleanup. Verified live on tablet (SM-X115): 5 post-deactivation server INTERRUPTED signals captured, each shows onInterrupted with voiceState=IDLE, state held.

title: Esp32Tap harness: full-sweep gates fail ~1-in-3 on a SATURATED host — the device's own TLS handshake budget firing
description:
SYMPTOM: running tools/sweep.sh back to back on this workstation, a single gate fails per run, a DIFFERENT one each time, always with a transport-level symptom and never with a logic assertion:

  run A  memreview FAIL  test_a_completed_quick_start_does_not_mark_another_program_completed
         'the DEVICE refused this TLS handshake: URLError(SSLEOFError...)'
         guest logged: E esp_https_server: esp_tls_create_server_session failed, 0xffff7ff7
         0xffff7ff7 = -ESP_ERR_ESP_TLS_SERVER_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT
  run B  program  FAIL  test_quick_start_runs_a_manual_program
         'UART1 capture reader STOPPED: UART1 capture socket closed by QEMU'
  DEEP   28/28 ALL GREEN in 1104s, program and memreview both included

CHARACTERISED: each of those two gates run 4x in ISOLATION on the same image passes 4/4. They only fail inside a full sweep, i.e. when the host is most loaded.

MECHANISM, for the TLS one, named by the device itself: net::http's handshake budget is a DELIBERATE belt-availability protection — a peer that completes TCP and then goes silent used to park the ONE httpd worker for the whole handshake (measured: Stop 0.25s -> 15.25s). Under host saturation the EMULATED ESP32-S3 is slow enough that a LEGITIMATE handshake exceeds that budget and the device correctly refuses it. That is the emulator being slow, not the firmware being wrong.

DO NOT 'FIX' THIS BY RAISING THE BUDGET OR ADDING A CLIENT RETRY. The budget is the protection; loosening it to make a gate pass is precisely the move this project forbids. The honest options are (a) run the sweep on a machine that is not also running a browser, a Postgres crawl and other agents (baseline load average here was ~10 of 20 cores BEFORE the sweep, with wezterm-gui at 45% CPU and a gmail-search crawl loop running), or (b) have the harness detect and REPORT host saturation rather than letting it masquerade as a firmware failure — e.g. record loadavg per gate and print it next to a failure, so the next person does not spend an investigation on it.

The UART1/QEMU-exit one is not yet mechanised; the container exit code is 137 for every session (the harness SIGKILLs on close, so it carries no signal) and there was no kernel OOM. It should be characterised the same way before anyone theorises about it.

NOT A REGRESSION FROM 55f592b/2d10da9: the same esp_tls_create_server_session HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT was observed on this tree BEFORE any of that work landed, during the reproduction runs for the coach intermittent.
close_reason: Duplicate of precor-9_3x-9aj, which already covers this class and is more complete. Evidence moved there as a comment.

title: Two QEMU suites go load-intermittent when the host is busy (load avg ~10)
description:
Both seen on 2026-07-29 in consecutive full sweeps, both PASS standalone
immediately afterwards, both are setup steps timing out rather than assertions
about behaviour:

  * test_mem_review.py::test_a_slow_reader_of_the_history_list_cannot_block_the
    _stop_button — "UART1 TX never contained b'[hmph:12C]' after 60s". The belt
    never reached 3.0 mph on the wire within the wait; 7/7 pass standalone at
    -n 4 (76 s) right after.
  * test_ble_degraded.py::test_the_belt_still_moves — see the separate bead;
    that one has a NAMED mechanism (the 4 s manual-lease deadman) and should be
    fixed there rather than here.

The common factor is the HOST, not the guest: `uptime` read load average 9.8
with another session running Chromium/playwright, a postgres pair and a
container loop on the same 20-core machine. Guest time under esp-QEMU lags wall
time badly and variably under load — the harness's own port-allocation comment
records a 121 s phantom "guest never booted" from the same cause — so a 60 s
wall-clock wait on a guest-observed fact can expire before the guest has done
60 s of work.

DO NOT "fix" this by raising the timeouts and DO NOT add retries. Two things
worth doing instead:
  1. Make the waits that are wall-clock into guest-clock waits where the
     harness can express that (QTSTATE carries `t_us`, the guest's own
     monotonic clock, and the session already parses it).
  2. Decide whether the sweep should refuse to start above a load threshold and
     say so, rather than producing a red gate that names the wrong file. A gate
     that fails for a reason outside the repository trains people to re-run it,
     which is how a real failure gets ignored.

Evidence that this is environmental and not a regression: the same tree passed a
full sweep (ALL GREEN, 566 s) and a DEEP sweep (ALL GREEN, 1084 s, 27 gates)
earlier the same morning when the machine was quiet.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text:
THIRD INSTANCE, and it is the cleanest example yet of this bead's own diagnosis:
the failure is a SETUP/PROBE WAIT expiring, not an assertion about behaviour.

2026-07-29, DEEP sweep at HEAD 0e5775c (the LittleFS power-loss work):

  test_adversarial.py::test_free_heap_converges_under_a_sustained_request_storm
  HarnessError: log pattern not seen: QTOK heap
  gate `adversar` ***FAIL*** 283s

`QT heap` is a three-accessor read-only probe answered by the qemu_test shim
task. "Pattern not seen" means the guest did not emit the ACK within cmd_ok's
15 s wall-clock wait while an HTTP storm was in flight — i.e. the shim task did
not get scheduled in 15 s of HOST time. Nothing was asserted about the heap at
all; the number never arrived.

Environmental, on this bead's own test: `uptime` read load average 7.2/7.7/8.2
immediately afterwards with a concurrent session on the same 20-core machine,
and the case passes STANDALONE right after — `-k storm` alone, 130 s, green. The
26 per-commit gates in that same DEEP run were all green, and the two full sweeps
immediately before it were ALL GREEN at 565 s and 568 s on the identical tree.

Same shape as the two cases already filed here (a wall-clock wait on a
guest-observed fact, expiring because guest time under esp-QEMU lags wall time
under load), and it extends the pattern past "waits for motor TX" to "waits for
any guest ACK". Both fixes this bead proposes would cover it: a guest-clock wait
(QTSTATE's `t_us`) instead of a wall-clock one, and/or a sweep that refuses to
start above a load threshold rather than producing a red gate that names the
wrong file.

Still: no retries, no raised timeouts.

comments.text:

title: test_ble_degraded::test_the_belt_still_moves is load-intermittent — the 4 s manual-lease deadman
description:
SEEN ONCE in a full sweep (2026-07-29, the sweep after the coach tier landed);
passes 3/3 standalone at -n 3 immediately afterwards, and passed in two earlier
full sweeps and one DEEP sweep the same morning. So: an intermittent, and the
mechanism is identifiable rather than mysterious — do NOT "fix" it with a sleep
or a retry.

    tools/qemu_scenarios/test_ble_degraded.py:205
    assert body["emu_speed"] == 30
    E   AssertionError: {'emu_speed': 0, 'emulate': False, ...}

The test POSTs /api/speed 3.0, asserts the REPLY says 30, then issues a second
GET /api/status and asserts 30 again. Between those two requests the belt can be
taken away by the 4 s MANUAL LEASE DEADMAN — which is a real, still-open defect
in its own right (test_reviewer_attacks.py::test_a_manual_speed_command_survives
_ten_seconds, red by design: "the belt was emergency-stopped by the 4 s manual
lease deadman with no ..."). The failure dict is that defect's exact signature:
speed 0 AND emulate False AND mode back to proxy, which is an emergency stop,
not a command that never landed.

Under load (a full sweep, xdist, a concurrent container) the gap between the two
requests can exceed 4 s, and then the assertion is asserting the absence of a
defect this repository already knows it has.

Two candidate fixes, in preference order:
  1. Fix the deadman (the real bug) — then the test is simply right.
  2. Until then, make the test's own window explicit: issue the second GET
     immediately and assert on a guest-observed fact (an audit event) rather
     than on a value that a 4 s timer is entitled to change.

NOT caused by the coach tier: the coach task idles at 100 ms priority 3 and
runs nothing at all unless a chat message is queued, and no coach scenario was
running in that sweep slot.

title: Android app: consume the ESP32 coach reply (202 + /ws coach frame), not the POST body
description:
The ESP32 answers POST /api/chat with 202 and an empty transcript; the answer arrives later as a /ws 'coach' frame and at GET /api/chat. The app handles neither, so the coach appears not to answer.

MEASURED SYMPTOM (worse than 'an empty bubble'): ChatSheet.kt:56-57 is onToast(res.text.ifBlank { 'No response' }) and Retrofit treats 202 as success, so every coach message toasted the literal words 'No response'. 55f592b makes the 202 body carry text='Thinking...' so an unchanged app degrades to a WAIT rather than to an error — that is a stopgap, not the fix.

STILL TO DO IN THE APP:
 1. ServerMessages.kt:16-31 selectDeserializer has no 'coach' case, so the frame falls to UnknownMessage and is logged and dropped. Add it, and render it in TreadmillViewModel.handleMessage.
 2. TreadmillApi.kt has no GET /api/chat at all — add it as the poll fallback for a client that missed the frame.
 3. A 429 ('I am still working on the last one.') is thrown by Retrofit as HttpException, so ChatSheet's .onFailure toasts 'Error connecting to AI' — a connectivity error from a device that is working correctly. Read the body on 429 and show its text. The firmware deliberately KEEPS the 429 status: answering 202 would claim a message was accepted that the device never queued, and hand the client somebody else's turn number to wait on.

All of it is a no-op against the Pi, which answers 200 with the full body and never sends a coach frame.

title: Esp32Tap coach: once-off manual confirmation against the LIVE Gemini endpoint
description:
The coach tier (net/coach.rs + coach_core) is proven deterministically against a
local stub in tools/qemu_scenarios/test_coach.py (18 cases, in the sweep). Three
things a stub CANNOT prove and that need one manual run against the real API:

  1. the request body coach_core::req builds is one generativelanguage.googleapis.com
     ACCEPTS (a stub answers whatever it likes regardless of what we sent);
  2. the embedded CA bundle (CONFIG_MBEDTLS_CERTIFICATE_BUNDLE_DEFAULT_FULL,
     68,983 bytes of flash) validates the real certificate chain — the stub is
     plain HTTP on purpose, because the key-pinning rule means a configurable
     endpoint never receives a key;
  3. the x-goog-api-key HEADER is the auth mechanism the endpoint honours (we
     deliberately do NOT put the key in the URL query).

How to run it (opt-in, deliberately NOT a gate — a live key, nondeterministic
words and somebody else's uptime is the definition of an intermittent):

    cd hardware/Esp32Tap/firmware/esp32_rs/tools/qemu_scenarios
    COACH_LIVE_KEY=<key> python3 -m pytest test_coach_live.py -q -s

The key comes from the environment only. Do NOT copy ./.gemini_key (the Pi's
per-device secret, gitignored and rsync-excluded) into the firmware tree or a
fixture.

Close this when a real turn has come back with real text and the console has
been checked for the key.

title: Esp32Tap: intermittent — memreview slow-reader case saw ZERO UART TX in one sweep run
description:
Observed ONCE, in one full sweep run, and not reproduced in 2 standalone runs of
the same file or in 3 later sweeps:

  test_mem_review.py::test_a_slow_reader_of_the_history_list_cannot_block_the_stop_button
  HarnessError: UART1 TX never contained b'[hmph:12C]' after offset 0 (have 0 bytes)

"have 0 bytes" means the guest emitted NO motor traffic at all in the 60 s
window — the device never entered emulate — rather than emitting the wrong
speed. The test had already loaded 20 maximal programs (~38 KB of history, so a
lot of flash work) and runs at -n 4.

MECHANISM NOT FOUND, and this is filed rather than shrugged at because an
intermittent costs an investigation every time and the investigations land on
wrong theories. The leading hypothesis is host starvation of the guest (four
QEMU containers plus a heavy flash-write phase), which would make it an artifact
of the harness rather than the firmware — but that is a hypothesis, not a
finding. Do NOT add a retry, a sleep, or a longer timeout to make it pass.

Next step: instrument the failing path to distinguish "the guest was starved"
from "the console pacer stopped feeding it" — the harness already reports
`pacer payloads sent=` in its dump, and in the failing run that number is the
thing to read first.

Not BLE-related: with bring-up refused, `ble::run` parks in a 60 s sleep loop
and no BLE code executes at all.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text:
SECOND OBSERVATION OF THE SAME SIGNATURE, in a DIFFERENT suite — and it kills
two elements of the leading hypothesis while pointing at a specific constant.

2026-07-29, sweep run 2 after the LittleFS power-loss work (HEAD a7a9e15):

  test_coach.py::test_a_generated_workout_lands_through_the_existing_program_path
  HarnessError: UART1 TX never contained b'[hmph:' after offset 0 (have 0 bytes)
  gate `coach` 44s -> 83s (the +39s IS the 60s wait_tx_contains timeout);
  every other gate in that sweep timed within 2s of the green run before it,
  so the host was NOT globally loaded.

WHAT THIS INSTANCE REMOVES FROM THE HYPOTHESIS:
  * NOT the flash-write phase. bwp's instance had just written ~38 KB of
    history; this test writes ONE history entry. The common factor is -n 4 and
    a belt, not flash volume.
  * NOT the pacer. The dump answers bwp's own "read this number first":
    `pacer payloads sent=615 pacer_error=None reader_error=None`.
  * NOT a starved-to-silence or crashed guest. The audit index advanced to 1243
    and the tail is solid `complete_console_frame`, so the guest was alive and
    parsing console frames for the whole 60 s window. No crash banner (the
    conftest crash check would have raised separately).

NOT REPRODUCED: test_coach.py -n 4 x3 all green (41-43 s), plus 4 rounds with an
instrumented duplicate of the failing test running alongside it (21 tests, -n 4)
all green. Same shape as bwp's original 0/2.

MECHANISM, NARROWED TO A NAMED CONSTANT (hypothesis, not yet caught in the act):
emulate entry is a multi-step transfer and TX_ENABLE is asserted WITHOUT sending
a byte (N12), so a transfer that fails emits ZERO motor bytes — which is exactly
"have 0 bytes" rather than a wrong speed. After `relay_cmd_on` the controller
gives the relay feedback RELAY_FEEDBACK_DEADLINE_US = 10 MILLISECONDS
(safety_core/src/safety/constants.rs:23); miss it and `enforce_due_safety` runs
`entry_feedback_timeout` with `fault_latched = true` (controller.rs:1260-1263).
That latch is UNRECOVERABLE (precor-9_3x-3yk), and `request_emulate` then refuses
every later attempt with `entry_rejected:fault_latched` (controller.rs:927) — so
ONE missed 10 ms window means no motor traffic for the REST of the session. A
guest vCPU descheduled for 10 ms while four QEMU containers share the host is
unremarkable, and QEMU's guest clock follows host time, so host contention
converts directly into a missed deadline. One mechanism explains all three filed
intermittents (this one, bwp's memreview case, a9y's ble_degraded case) and
explains why none of them recovers within its session.

THE INSTRUMENT THAT WOULD SETTLE IT, and why the evidence is missing today: the
controller ALREADY names the reason — one of
`entry_rejected:{not_owner,not_proxy,fault_latched,tread_not_ok,
feedback_not_bypass,console_not_fresh,uart_not_idle_low}`, plus
`entry_feedback_timeout` / `entry_abort:no_gap` / `feedback_window_stalled`. It
is invisible only because `debug_dump()` prints the LAST 40 audit events of a
ring flooded at ~5/s by `complete_console_frame`. `QemuSession.audit_events()`
returns the WHOLE ring, so the fix belongs in the scenario, not the harness
(tools/qemu_harness/ is byte-locked by verify_harness_copy.py): on a
wait_tx_contains failure, print `s.state()` (QTSTATE carries fault=) and
`[t for _, t in s.audit_events() if "entry" in t or "fault" in t]`. Any suite
whose test waits on motor TX should do that — it turns the next occurrence from
an investigation into one line of output.

Still: do NOT add a retry, a sleep, or a longer timeout.

title: Esp32Tap: replace hand-rolled recstore with LittleFS
description:
recstore/ is a hand-rolled fixed-record flash store. LittleFS handles power-loss resilience, atomic metadata and wear levelling as its headline features and would mean owning far less code — it is the conventional answer.

BLOCKER (tried, reverted, ~4 build probes): esp-idf-sys's stock bindings.h only #includes headers for components it knows about, guarded by ESP_IDF_COMP_<NAME>_ENABLED. That is why espressif/mdns needed nothing extra. joltwallet/littlefs is third-party and absent from that list, so adding it via extra_components BUILDS the component but yields ZERO symbols. It needs a custom bindings_header; declaring one in [package.metadata.esp-idf-sys] did not take effect (metadata parsed, key absent from the esp-idf-sys table at build time). Solve THAT, then delete recstore rather than extending it.

EVIDENCE THIS MATTERS: writing recstore produced two real defects within an hour, both caught by its own torn-write test — (1) slots packed 16-to-a-sector meant erasing one destroyed the other 15, because NOR erase granularity is 4 KB; (2) a torn header left the erased 0xFFFFFFFF sequence reading as the NEWEST valid record, and the unchecked seq+1 overflowed under panic=abort, which reboots the device and drops the relay. LittleFS would have had neither.

Citation: esp-idf-sys 0.37.2 BUILD-OPTIONS.md lines 386-458 ('Extra ESP-IDF components') plus lines 88-95 (root-crate-only note). Verified: libjoltwallet__littlefs.a actually compiled under target/.../esp-idf-sys-*/out/build/esp-idf/joltwallet__littlefs/, and bindings.rs grew a 'pub mod littlefs_probe { ... pub fn esp_vfs_littlefs_register(conf: *const esp_vfs_littlefs_conf_t) -> esp_err_t; ... }' block with real symbols (not empty). comments.author: Claude
comments.text:
DONE — recstore DELETED, LittleFS live behind the unchanged `Stores` API, commit 63d4691 on worktree-esp32tap-firmware.

THE BLOCKER: a misplaced key, not a missing capability. `bindings_header` is a field on each [[package.metadata.esp-idf-sys.extra_components]] ENTRY, not a key on the [package.metadata.esp-idf-sys] TABLE — the earlier attempt set it on the table, where no such key exists, which is precisely why it 'parsed but was absent at build time'. Fix is one line of TOML plus esp32tap/bindings/littlefs.h guarded by ESP_IDF_COMP_JOLTWALLET__LITTLEFS_ENABLED (slash -> double underscore, same convention as espressif/mdns). Component pinned at joltwallet/littlefs 1.22.3 in components_esp32s3.lock. Citation: esp-idf-sys 0.37.2 BUILD-OPTIONS.md lines 386-458 + 88-95.

WHAT LANDED: 772 lines of recstore/src/lib.rs plus its Cargo files and its sweep gate are gone; no compatibility shim, no second store. net/store.rs is now files on a real filesystem, one atomic rename per write (lfs_rename is a single metadata commit, so a power cut leaves the previous content — never half-written, never missing, never duplicated; strictly better than recstore's erase-then-write, which documented its loss window as acceptable). The module still owns a 4-byte sequence per record because a filesystem has no notion of 'the third-newest record' and every list endpoint needs one — but no magic, no length, no CRC, no torn-write recovery: integrity is the filesystem's job now. Only net/store.rs and net/profile.rs ever named recstore::, so the endpoints did not change.

MEMORY, MEASURED NOT ESTIMATED (the number this bead asked for): resident = 992 bytes = 200 index + 792 mount, read out of a live guest via QT store_stat. The 200 is exact and is EXACTLY what the three recstore rings held (size_of::<Index<20>>*2 + size_of::<Index<4>> = 88+88+24). The 792 is the mount, measured by sampling free heap either side of esp_vfs_littlefs_register and latching the difference, so it is this device's figure rather than arithmetic. NET COST OF THE SWAP: +792 bytes, paid once at boot, constant in stored volume, record size and request count. Buffers sized explicitly in sdkconfig.defaults — CACHE_SIZE 128 (not the component's 512) x2, LOOKAHEAD 32 (sized to the 256-block partition, not the default 128), MAX_PARTITIONS 1, no mtime (no RTC to trust), no SPIFFS compat, and deliberately NO CONFIG_LITTLEFS_WDT_RESET because petting the WDT inside a flash op hides exactly the stall that must reach it.

UNSAFE WENT DOWN, 1200 -> 1180 lines: recstore needed the whole esp_partition_* surface behind a Flash trait plus an unsafe impl Send; LittleFS needs a mount and nothing else, and every read/write/rename/unlink below it is std::fs. Two unsafe sites remain in store.rs, both with SAFETY comments, both allowlisted in check_unsafe_budget.py.

ACCEPTANCE PROOF, UNEDITED: test_records.py and test_store_persistence.py pass with ZERO edits (verified: git diff HEAD against both is empty) — saved workout survives a reboot, history dedups by name and holds its cap of 20, a run is created past 5 s / checkpointed in place past 30 s / finalised, a profile rename survives a reboot, resident memory does not move across 240 writes + full list reads. Full sweep 25 gates ALL GREEN in 560 s (records 167 s, storepers 9 s). The 'run recstore' sweep gate was removed rather than replaced: what stands in as evidence is storepers + records, which run against real flash in a real guest and were not touched by the swap.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text:
FOLLOW-UP LANDED (78758ec, a7a9e15) — the swap's evidence gap closed.

The migration commit (63d4691) replaced recstore's TWO torn-write tests with an
argument from littlefs's design and nothing else, so the persistence tier briefly
had ZERO power-loss coverage: every acceptance test reboots with `QT reboot`,
which is a CLEAN esp_restart AFTER the write completed. That is now measured:

  * `QT store_tear <point> <off> <n> <payload>` resets the SoC INSIDE
    `write_slot` — mid-staging at a chosen byte, after the sync and before the
    rename, and just after the rename. esp_restart is a soft reset and QEMU's
    flash image outlives it, so the next boot re-mounts the littlefs a real cut
    would leave.
  * tools/qemu_scenarios/test_store_power_loss.py (gate `storetorn`, 8 s, 7
    cases) asserts the slot reads EXACTLY the old record or EXACTLY the new one,
    that the count never moves, that the store still mounts, and that the next
    write still lands. The in-place path is used deliberately — an interrupted
    append can only leave a free slot empty.

Three defects found while doing it, all fixed in 78758ec:
  * `write_slot` DISCARDED the close result. `write_all` returning Ok only
    reaches littlefs's 128-byte file cache; the size and block pointers commit
    at `lfs_file_sync`, and File::Drop throws close's error away — so a failed
    commit would have renamed a short-or-empty file over a good record. Now
    `sync_all()` gates the rename.
  * `erase_nth` cleared the index on a FAILED unlink, behind a comment asserting
    the opposite of what happens: the file IS still there, so mount() read its
    sequence back and RESURRECTED the deleted record while the client was told
    NOT_FOUND. It now finishes the delete by zeroing the slot header through the
    same atomic rename, or leaves the index alone so RAM and flash agree.
  * The "one atomic metadata commit" claim was silently conditional on TMP and
    every slot sharing the mount ROOT. `same_dir` pins it (const assert on TMP,
    debug_assert on every destination).

Also: `resident_bytes` -> `mount_cost_bytes`. Both its terms are latched at boot,
so the equality the acceptance test asserts on it is true by construction and
would pass through a per-write leak. It is the mount's price tag (992 bytes = 200
index + 792 mount); the anti-growth property is carried by the free heap, which
`QT store_stat` now reports beside it (`heap=`). And CONFIG_LITTLEFS_BLOCK_CYCLES
is stated explicitly with the checkpoint-cadence erase budget rather than left at
the component default inside a block that claims to state every cost.

The acceptance tests were NOT edited: `git diff 63d4691 HEAD` over
test_records.py and test_store_persistence.py is empty.

title: run fingerprint is timing-dependent once a plan is reshaped mid-run
description:
Found by codex during the skip-truncation review (see precor-9_3x-2vs sibling).

_program_fingerprint (server.py:364) hashes interval durations. The run record captures it at _start_run_record (~30s into a session) and later updates never rewrite it. Now that skip truncates durations (and extend/split already resized them), a skip BEFORE the record is inserted stores the truncated fingerprint, while a skip AFTER stores the original. So whether a run joins back to its saved workout depends purely on when the skip happened.

Options: fingerprint the plan as loaded (retain the original alongside the live one), or fingerprint on something reshape-invariant.

Impact: 'how did I do last time on this workout' / saved-workout-to-run attribution, not belt control.

title: prev() rewinds the program clock behind real elapsed time
description:
Counterpart to the skip fix (skip now truncates the interval being left so plan time == real time). prev() still rebases total_elapsed backward to the previous interval's start while the session wall clock keeps running, so the two desync in the other direction: the ridgeline marker jumps back to a milestone the timer has already passed.

Options: (a) prev inserts a fresh copy of the previous interval at the current position (timeline grows, clocks stay in sync, matches 'run that one again'); (b) prev restores the duration a prior skip truncated, making skip->prev a clean roundtrip; (c) leave as-is and accept the asymmetry.

prev is a prominent control (both sides of the RidgelineHud), so this is user-reachable.

title: Layout jitter when encouragement text changes font size
description: When encouragement/milestone messages appear with smaller font, the screen shrinks and grows, causing visible layout jitter. The layout should remain stable regardless of message content — use fixed-height containers or min-height so the surrounding UI doesn't shift.

title: Add 'My Workouts' section for saved user workouts
description: Add a 'My Workouts' section to the UI (both web and Android) where users can save, name, and re-use their favorite workout programs. Currently program_history.json stores recent programs (max 10, auto-rotated), but there's no way to explicitly save/favorite a workout for permanent access. This feature should include: (1) ability to 'save' a completed or generated program to a persistent favorites list, (2) a 'My Workouts' UI section accessible from the idle/lobby screen, (3) ability to rename saved workouts, (4) ability to delete saved workouts, (5) API endpoints for CRUD on saved workouts, (6) persistent storage (separate from program_history.json). Dual-platform: web UI + Android app.

title: Timer flickers on orientation change (grows/shrinks)

title: Harden deploy backup retention configuration
description: deploy/deploy.sh accepts KEEP_BACKUPS=0, creates the predeploy snapshot, then immediately deletes it while allowing deployment to continue. If the snapshot guarantee is intentional, validate KEEP_BACKUPS as an integer >=1 and add focused coverage for zero/non-numeric values.

title: Verify Ridgeline camera-pan transition on Galaxy Tab
description: The 2026-08-22 physical-device landing run verified sustained marker motion, sticky labels, steepness, lens appearance, and skip reshaping, but could not reach the first camera-pan threshold near 492 seconds because skip preserves elapsed time and there is no public fast-forward. Add a safe test hook or long-running device scenario and capture the actual pan while checking lens/labels remain aligned.
acceptance_criteria: Physical-device evidence covers a camera window transition with marker, lens, transition ticks, labels, and leader lines remaining aligned throughout.

title: Strengthen Ridgeline presentation and fallback tests
description: Landing review found that the realistic 61-label test exempts overlapFallback slots but does not assert zero fallbacks, and lens tests cover arithmetic rather than draw ordering/gating/alignment. Add realistic no-fallback assertions plus render/screenshot coverage for short vs windowed routes and camera/canvas changes; automate final composited contrast where practical.
acceptance_criteria: Representative supported routes assert no avoidable fallback/overlap; presentation tests cover lens gating, ordering, clipping, and camera alignment; contrast validation covers the composited result.

title: Clean up ProgramState async test teardown
description: The full Python gate passes but emits six warnings that ProgramState tick-loop tasks are still pending during test_workout_session.py teardown. Make fixtures stop/await the background tasks deterministically so real coroutine leaks remain visible.
acceptance_criteria: Full Python suite completes without pending/destroyed ProgramState task warnings and without sleeps/retries masking teardown.

title: no size limit on client-supplied program in POST /api/workouts
description:
Found by codex during the skip-truncation review. Pre-existing, not introduced by that change.

SaveWorkoutRequest.program (server.py:754) is an unrestricted dict and _validate_program (server.py:517) only checks that duration/speed/incline are numeric — it accepts zero and negative durations, and there is no cap on interval count or payload size. The dict is json.dumps'd into program_history/saved_workouts, and update_history_entry now rewrites it too. SQL is parameterized (no injection), so this is a resource-exhaustion / data-quality issue rather than an injection one.

Suggested: cap interval count and reject duration <= 0 in _validate_program.
notes: 2026-08-23 landing review: current _validate_program calls math.isfinite() directly on arbitrary JSON integers; sufficiently large finite Python ints raise OverflowError instead of returning a validation error. Cover huge numeric magnitudes while adding the already-planned size/count limits.

title: Esp32Tap: no WS 'kv' frames from native server tier — app Debug screen empty on-device
description: python/server.py broadcasts every console/motor KV pair on /ws (type 'kv') and a status frame per C++ status event; the ESP32 native tier only sends status/session/program frames from endpoint handlers and the 1 Hz tick. Kotlin handleKVUpdate feeds the Debug screen kvLog + live motor map from kv frames — both stay empty on the standalone device, and proxy-mode live speed/incline only refreshes on connect/API events (GET /api/status polling does decode hmph/inc correctly). Consider a rate-limited kv/status push from the serial engine's MotorKvCache.

title: Esp32Tap: pre-existing sdkconfig 2MB-flash bug fixed in the server-tier workflow
description: hardware/Esp32Tap/firmware/esp32 was configured CONFIG_ESPTOOLPY_FLASHSIZE_2MB + single 1MB factory app even though the BOM module is ESP32-S3-WROOM-1-N8 (8 MB). Fixed: CONFIG_ESPTOOLPY_FLASHSIZE_8MB + custom partitions_esp32tap.csv (2 MB factory, 1 MB LittleFS 'storage'). Close-on-land note: nothing further to do; this issue records the fix for the flashed-device migration story (existing dev boards need a full reflash including the new partition table).

title: Esp32Tap: /api/runs endpoint deliberately omitted from the native server
description: python/server.py exposes GET /api/runs but kotlin TreadmillApi.kt never references it (run records ARE consumed via the embedded last_run field on history/workout entries, which the native server provides). If a future app version adds a runs screen, expose the RunStore array as GET /api/runs. Currently 404s.

title: digikey CLI: natural-language search fails on mid-obscurity parts
description: 'digikey search "Omron G6K-2F-Y DPDT relay"' returns 0 matches; the bare manufacturer part number 'G6K-2F-Y-TR DC5' resolves fine. The README's examples ('10k 0603 resistor', 'wifi module') are the easy end of the spectrum, so the docs oversell search as a discovery tool for parts whose MPN you do not already know. Also seen: the relay's row displays manufacturer 'Aratas America LLC' (a reseller) rather than Omron, so an agent cross-checking 'is this the part I asked for' against the manufacturer name will wrongly reject a correct match.
acceptance_criteria: README/--help set honest expectations about what search can and cannot find, and note that the Manufacturer column may show a reseller rather than the original maker.
close_reason: Migrated to the standalone digikey-api repo (github.com/scottmsilver/digikey-api): 09i→digikey-api-s61, gxc→digikey-api-xvq. This project no longer lives in treddy.

title: Finish or drop: lock_emulate IPC flag (suppress auto-proxy on console press)
description: Unfinished work rescued from the deleted sorted-rolling-church worktree (uncommitted, ~36 lines): a lock_emulate flag on ModeStateMachine + IPC command parsing + treadmill_client.py support. Purpose: suppress auto-proxy-on-console-change so console button events flow through while emulate stays active. Full patch preserved in notes.

title: Engine parity: muted() clamp exists in TS but not Kotlin; golden coverage too thin
description: engine.ts harmonizePalette clamps tint L<=0.32,C<=0.06 via muted(); Engine.kt omits it (no-op at current seeds, latent divergence if constants change). golden.json themes don't exercise achromatic dominant, dark-polarity prior, out-of-gamut tint, or fallback. EngineTest only checks tint.r +-1.0 vs TS exact match. Port muted() to Kotlin (or inline both), add golden cases, tighten EngineTest tolerance.

title: PhotoSampler.bgAt does a full per-pixel scan + HashMap alloc in onGloballyPositioned every layout pass
description: LegibleGlassPanel samples in onGloballyPositioned; sampleRegionPixels builds a throwaway color-bucket HashMap though bgAt only uses .avg. During timer/encouragement animations this is a per-frame alloc+scan in a layout callback. Memoize by quantized bounds, sparse-stride sample, or skip the dominant bucket map for avg-only.

title: Engine samples full bitmap but screen uses ContentScale.Crop — sampled rects don't match rendered pixels
description: On-device verification (emulator, bright bg_forest) showed the hero timer scrim works and is legible, but the metrics row secondary text reads faint over a bright crop. Root cause: rememberRunReadability() samples the FULL decoded bg_forest bitmap at normalized rects, while RunningScreen draws it with ContentScale.Crop (fillMaxSize). On a phone aspect ratio the crop discards top/bottom (or sides), so the pixels actually behind each text block differ from what the engine sampled — the APCA guarantee becomes approximate. Fix: sample the SAME crop the UI renders (compute the crop rect for the device aspect ratio and map block rects into it), or sample after layout from the displayed region. Found during feat/adaptive-text-readability emulator QA.
close_reason: Fixed: cropMapRect maps block rects through ContentScale.Crop before sampling; pure + unit-tested; verified on emulator (portrait+landscape).

title: Wire BackgroundAdviceClient to runtime so the Gemini prior reaches the device
description: rememberRunReadability() in RunningScreen.kt currently calls chooseTheme(regions, AdvicePrior()) with a hardcoded neutral prior — the server endpoint /api/background/advise and the Kotlin BackgroundAdviceClient both exist and are tested, but are not connected. Fetch the prior off the main thread (keyed by sha256 of the background image, which is also the server cache key) and recompute the Theme when it returns, behind a remember keyed on the prior so neutral renders first then refines. APCA already guarantees legibility without it; this only adds photo-matched hue/polarity. From feat/adaptive-text-readability.

title: Remove legacy GlassParams brightness path (rememberGlassParams/fromBrightness/sampleBrightness/overlayOpacity)
description: After the adaptive-readability engine landed, the old global-average brightness model in GlassTheme.kt is fully dead: rememberGlassParams(), GlassParams.fromBrightness(), GlassParams.sampleBrightness(), and the overlayOpacity field have no remaining callers. Remove them (and now-unused imports: BitmapFactory/Bitmap/LocalContext/remember/Composable) and update the GlassParams class docstring which still describes the brightness-driven model. Keeping two parallel readability systems invites drift. Flagged by final code review on feat/adaptive-text-readability.

title: Correct + finish mDNS device-discovery spec
description: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-05-18-mdns-device-discovery-design.md draft has a wrong claim ('both native clients accept self-signed with zero client changes' — Android required trustAllTls()). Correct it: Android needed a trust-all X509TrustManager; iOS already correct. Add explicit prerequisite note: the scheme=https TXT is valid only because HTTPS-on-commissioned-Pis (precor-9_3x-41a) shipped. Then resume the brainstorming review gate -> writing-plans.
close_reason: mDNS spec corrected: false 'zero client changes' TLS claim fixed (Android needed trustAllTls; iOS already correct), HTTPS prerequisite section added (precor-9_3x-41a satisfied). Self-review passed. Spec is at the brainstorming user-review gate before writing-plans.

The workout_session already tracks cumulative vertical feet, so we can compute remaining from the program's total expected vert.

close_reason: Removed 'remaining of' text block from portrait RunningScreen and cleaned up unused fmtDur import

title: Esp32Tap: profile avatars unsupported on-device (POST 501) — decide store-or-drop
description: Native profile tier answers GET /api/profiles/{id}/avatar 404 'No avatar' and POST 501; has_avatar always false, so the unchanged app never renders avatars on the standalone device. If avatars are wanted, they need a bounded LittleFS blob store (python caps uploads at 1 MB — too big for the 1 MB /data partition; would need downscaling).

title: Landscape: timer/encouragement block duplicated; displayCutout only handles top edge
description: RunningScreen portrait timer/encouragement (~80 lines incl. exempt Text) is copy-pasted into the landscape variant; rememberRunReadability re-decodes per orientation. Also windowInsetsPadding uses displayCutout.only(Top) in landscape, so a side punch-hole isn't avoided. Hoist the shared block + use all-sides cutout/safeContent in landscape.

title: Apply per-region scrims to individual metric tiles (not one shared metricsScrim)
description: rememberRunReadability() computes per-region scrim alphas for speed/incline/distance/hint but only scrims['speed'] is used to drive the shared LocalGlassParams.panelOpacity, so every metric tile gets the same scrim. The engine's per-region precision is mostly unused for the metric row. Consider providing per-tile scrim (e.g. a CompositionLocal map or passing scrim into each tile) so each tile clears its own local APCA target. Low priority — tiles sit in one row over similar background, so the shared scrim is usually adequate. From feat/adaptive-text-readability.

title: Make Kotlin parseAdvicePrior per-field tolerant (match Python coercion)
description: BackgroundAdviceClient.parseAdvicePrior uses a single try/catch so one bad field (e.g. non-numeric palette_hue) discards the entire prior, unlike the Python advise_background which coerces each field independently. Safe today (returns AdvicePrior() defaults, never crashes) but less granular. Make each field parse independently. Minor, from final review on feat/adaptive-text-readability.

title: BLE WiFi onboarding (screenless first-network setup)
description: Future option from the mDNS spec: BLE solves zero-network onboarding (push WiFi creds to a screenless treadmill before it can be on the LAN); mDNS then handles steady-state. Non-blocking, out of scope for the mDNS plan. See docs/superpowers/specs/2026-05-18-mdns-device-discovery-design.md (Out of scope section).

title: Android: AnimatedContent may flash empty text during encouragement exit animation
description:
In RunningScreen.kt, AnimatedContent now keys on encouragement != null (Boolean) to avoid bounce animation on every countdown tick. However, inside the showEncouragement == true branch, the code reads encouragement directly from compose state rather than from the animated target state.

During the exit animation (encouragement to timer transition), encouragement may already be null while the exit animation is still rendering. glowText(encouragement ?: "") would briefly show empty text before the fade completes.

Impact: Unlikely to be visible given the fast spring animation (dampingRatio=0.6f), but could cause a brief blank flash if the device is under load.

Affected code: RunningScreen.kt lines ~157 and ~424 (portrait and landscape).

Potential fix: Cache the last non-null encouragement value in a remember block and use that inside the AnimatedContent lambda, so the exit animation always has text to display.
